source.title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p and order q, and let s be an integer coprime to q − 1 so that the power map x ↦ x^s is a permutation of L. Define the Weil sum W_{L,s}(a) = Σ_{x∈L} μ(x^s − ax), where μ is the canonical additive character of L. Call the exponent s singular if there exists a nonzero a ∈ L such that W_{L,s}(a) = 0. If |L| > 2 and s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), must s always be singular? Equivalently, must there always exist some a ∈ L× for which the corresponding Weil sum vanishes?
accepted.context_brief: Helleseth vanishing conjecture for Weil sums

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1.1 (Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture, 1976). If |L| > 2 and s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), then s is singular.
Conjecture 2.3 (Helleseth’s 1976 Vanishing Conjecture, restated). Let s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1) be an integer coprime to q − 1. The rank of the matrix [µ((x − y)^s)]_{y,x∈L} is less than q − 1.

accepted.question_text: Take p ∈ {2, 3} and let L be a finite field of characteristic p and order q. For the exponent s = q − 2, which satisfies s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1) exactly in these two characteristics, can one prove the Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture for this case without using the theory of elliptic curves? In other words, can one show by a different method that there exists a nonzero a ∈ L such that W_{L,q−2}(a) = 0?
accepted.context_brief: Avoid elliptic-curve proof for the q−2 case

evidence.quote: Problem 1.2. Prove the Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture for p ∈ {2, 3} and s = q − 2 without using of the theory of elliptic curves.

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p such that the extension degree [L : F_p] is a power of two, and let s be an invertible exponent, meaning gcd(s, |L| − 1) = 1. Is it true that the reduced Fourier spectrum of the power map x ↦ x^s can never take exactly three distinct values? Equivalently, whenever [L : F_p] is a power of two, must every invertible exponent fail to be three-valued?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1.5 (Helleseth Three-Valued Conjecture, 1976). For any prime p, if [L : F_p] is a power of two, then the spectrum of an invertible exponent is not three-valued.
This conjecture remains open for p > 3.

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite field and let f : L → L be a map, or more specifically a permutation. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which scalar multiplication of the output by any nonzero field element preserves the spectrum: for every b ∈ L×, the map bf defined by (bf)(x) = b f(x) has exactly the same Fourier spectrum as f. Which maps or permutations have this spectrum-invariance property for all nonzero scalars b?
accepted.context_brief: Characterize spectrum invariance under output scaling

evidence.quote: Problem 3.1 (invariance). Find necessary and sufficient conditions for a map (or permutation) f : L → L to have the property that the spectrum of f is equal to the spectrum of bf for all b ∈ L×.

accepted.question_text: Let L be a finite field of order q > 2, and let f be a power permutation of L with exponent s satisfying s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), where p is the characteristic. Aubry and Langevin proved that there exists a nonzero a ∈ L such that the Fourier coefficient f̂(a) is divisible by 3. Can one prove an analogous divisibility theorem involving some other prime ℓ different from the characteristic p?
accepted.context_brief: Divisibility of Fourier coefficients by primes ℓ ≠ p

evidence.quote: Theorem 3.3 (Aubry, Langevin, 2013). Let L be a finite field of order q > 2. If f is a power permutation of L of exponent s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), then there is an a ∈ L× such that f̂(a) ≡ 0 (mod 3).
Problem 3.4. Is it possible to obtain such a divisibility result involving another prime ℓ ≠ p?

accepted.question_text: Suppose x ↦ x^s is a power permutation of a finite field and its spectrum takes exactly four distinct values. Is there an analogue of Theorem 3.5, the theorem that in the three-valued case forces singularity, integrality, and the congruence s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1)? More concretely, what structural restrictions must hold for four-valued exponents, parallel to the ones known for three-valued exponents?
accepted.context_brief: Four-valued analogue of Katz’s three-valued theorem

evidence.quote: Theorem 3.5 (Katz, 2012). If x^s is a three-valued power permutation, then s is singular, s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), and the spectrum {0, A, B} of x^s lies in Z.
Problem 3.6. Find an analogue of Theorem 3.5 for four-valued exponents.

accepted.question_text: Let F(x) = μ(x^s) for a power map on a finite field, and let A_1, …, A_n denote the nonzero values in the spectrum of F. For which exponents s is the product of the nonzero spectral values, ∏_{i=1}^n A_i, divisible by q, the size of the field?
accepted.context_brief: Divisibility of product of nonzero spectral values

evidence.quote: Problem 3.7 (product). For which s is the product of non-zero spectral values ∏_{i=1}^n A_i of F(x) = µ(x^s) divisible by q?

accepted.question_text: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, and write s ≉ 1 to mean that s is not equivalent to 1 under the equivalence generated by s′ ≡ p^j s (mod q − 1) and inversion. Call s nice when the number N(1, v) of solutions to x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v takes at most three values as v ranges over the field. The authors found by computation that all nice exponents s ≉ 1 over prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 come from the paradigmatic families in Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Does every nice exponent s ≉ 1 arise from those paradigmatic examples?
accepted.context_brief: Classify all nice exponents beyond the known families

evidence.quote: Definition 6.1. Let s be an invertible exponent over the finite field L. We say that s is a nice exponent over L if the number N(1, v) of solutions in L^2 of x + y = 1, x^s + y^s = v, takes at most 3 values as v runs through L.

Problem 6.7. All nice exponents s ≉ 1 over the prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 were found in the numerical experiment [15], and they all correspond to the paradigmatic examples of Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Is this a general property?

accepted.question_text: Let s be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, assume s ≉ 1, and suppose s is nice in the sense that the differential multiplicity counts N(1, v) take at most three values as v varies. Must 2 always occur as one of the differential multiplicities of s?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 6.8 (nice exponent). Let s ≉ 1 be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic. If s is nice, then 2 is a differential multiplicity.

accepted.question_text: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, and assume s ≉ 1. Must 2 always occur as a differential multiplicity of s? That is, for every such invertible exponent, does there always exist some v for which the number N(1, v) of solutions to x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v equals 2?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 6.9 (optimist). Let s ≉ 1 be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic. If s is invertible, then 2 is a differential multiplicity.
